claim: GFP-CBX2 was properly incorporated in the PRC1 complex in K562 GFP-CBX2 cells.
source: GFP pull out experiments in K562 GFP-CBX2 cells confirmed that GFP-CBX2 was properly incorporated in the PRC1 complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GFP pull-out experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: GFP-CBX2 target genes largely overlapped with endogenous CBX2 target genes based on ENCODE/Broad Institute data.
source: ChIP-seq experiments in K562 GFP-CBX2 and K562 wild-type cells showed that GFP-CBX2 target genes largely overlapped with endogenous CBX2 target genes (based on ENCODE/Broad Institute data) and H2AK119ub enriched genes (van den Boom et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq experimental data comparing GFP-CBX2 and endogenous CBX2 target genes, with reference to published data

claim: GFP-CBX2 target genes overlapped with H2AK119ub enriched genes.
source: ChIP-seq experiments in K562 GFP-CBX2 and K562 wild-type cells showed that GFP-CBX2 target genes largely overlapped with endogenous CBX2 target genes (based on ENCODE/Broad Institute data) and H2AK119ub enriched genes (van den Boom et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq experimental data with reference to published work

claim: GFP-CBX2 fusion protein is incorporated into a fully functional PRC1 complex.
source: These data underline that the GFP-CBX2 fusion protein is incorporated into a fully functional PRC1 complex.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing proper incorporation and target gene overlap

claim: GFP-CBX2 was homogenously distributed throughout the nucleus in untreated cord blood CD34+ cells.
source: Whereas GFP-CBX2 was homogenously distributed throughout the nucleus in untreated cells, cells that received a HS (30 min, 44°C) displayed strong accumulations of GFP-CBX2 in subnuclear domains, both in cells that were fixed after HS (Figure 1B) and living cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and 1C

claim: Cells that received a heat shock (30 min, 44°C) displayed strong accumulations of GFP-CBX2 in subnuclear domains.
source: Whereas GFP-CBX2 was homogenously distributed throughout the nucleus in untreated cells, cells that received a HS (30 min, 44°C) displayed strong accumulations of GFP-CBX2 in subnuclear domains, both in cells that were fixed after HS (Figure 1B) and living cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in fixed and living cells shown in Figures 1B and 1C

claim: K562 leukemic cells showed HS-induced relocalization of GFP-CBX2 to subnuclear domains.
source: Similarly, K562 leukemic cells also showed HS-induced relocalization of GFP-CBX2 to subnuclear domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: HS induces relocalization of GFP-CBX2 to nucleoli.
source: Transmission images suggested that HS induces relocalization of GFP-CBX2 to nucleoli, which was confirmed by immunofluorescence analyses using antibodies against the nucleolar proteins NPM1 and Fibrillarin (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by transmission microscopy and immunofluorescence data shown in multiple figures

claim: GFP-CBX2 localized directly around Fibrillarin, which is confined to the dense fibrillar component (DFC) of the nucleolus.
source: GFP-CBX2 localized directly around Fibrillarin, which is confined to the dense fibrillar component (DFC) of the nucleolus, and partially colocalized with the granular component (GC) protein NPM1.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data and established knowledge about Fibrillarin localization

claim: GFP-CBX2 partially colocalized with the granular component (GC) protein NPM1.
source: GFP-CBX2 localized directly around Fibrillarin, which is confined to the dense fibrillar component (DFC) of the nucleolus, and partially colocalized with the granular component (GC) protein NPM1.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data and established knowledge about NPM1 localization

claim: GFP-CBX2 is most enriched in the granular component of the nucleolus.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that GFP-CBX2 is most enriched in the granular component of the nucleolus (Boisvert et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from colocalization data with reference to published work on nucleolar structure

claim: The kinetics of HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of GFP-CBX2 were dependent on the duration of the HS.
source: The kinetics of HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of GFP-CBX2 were both dependent on the duration and temperature of the HS (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures

claim: The kinetics of HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of GFP-CBX2 were dependent on the temperature of the HS.
source: The kinetics of HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of GFP-CBX2 were both dependent on the duration and temperature of the HS (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures

claim: Cells exposed to a temperature of 42°C displayed nucleolar localization of GFP-CBX2 albeit with slower kinetics.
source: Cells exposed to a temperature of 42°C also displayed nucleolar localization of GFP-CBX2 albeit with slower kinetics.
evidence: Supported by kinetic experimental data comparing different temperatures

claim: All CBX paralogs (GFP-CBX4, GFP-CBX6, GFP-CBX7, GFP-CBX8) displayed HS-induced nucleolar accumulation.
source: Indeed, all these CBX paralogs displayed HS-induced nucleolar accumulation (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 1F and 1G

claim: Endogenous CBX4 showed nucleolar accumulation upon HS in K562 cells.
source: Importantly, using immunofluorescence, we also observed nucleolar accumulation of endogenous CBX4 upon HS, both in K562 and HL60 cells (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H and supplementary figure

claim: Endogenous CBX4 showed nucleolar accumulation upon HS in HL60 cells.
source: Importantly, using immunofluorescence, we also observed nucleolar accumulation of endogenous CBX4 upon HS, both in K562 and HL60 cells (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in supplementary figure

claim: The homology between various CBX proteins is confined to the chromodomain (N-terminus) and Pc box (C-terminus).
source: Since the homology between these various CBX proteins is confined to the chromodomain (N-terminus) and Pc box (C-terminus), we generated GFP-CBX2 and GFP-CBX8 fusions only containing the chromobox (GFP-CBX2 [2-63]) or the chromobox and AT hook (GFP-CBX2 [2-96]) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CBX protein structure

claim: All generated truncated GFP-CBX fusion proteins displayed nucleolar localization after HS.
source: Strikingly, all generated truncated GFP-CBX fusion proteins displayed nucleolar localization after HS, suggesting the presence of the chromodomain is sufficient to induce nucleolar localization after HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: The presence of the chromodomain is sufficient to induce nucleolar localization after HS.
source: Strikingly, all generated truncated GFP-CBX fusion proteins displayed nucleolar localization after HS, suggesting the presence of the chromodomain is sufficient to induce nucleolar localization after HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data with truncated constructs

claim: The kinetics of HS-induced relocalization of truncated CBX proteins were slightly slower than full-length proteins.
source: The kinetics of HS-induced relocalization of truncated CBX proteins were slightly slower, suggesting that also non-homologous peptide stretches in CBX proteins contribute to nucleolar relocalization.
evidence: Supported by kinetic experimental data comparing truncated and full-length proteins

claim: Non-homologous peptide stretches in CBX proteins contribute to nucleolar relocalization.
source: The kinetics of HS-induced relocalization of truncated CBX proteins were slightly slower, suggesting that also non-homologous peptide stretches in CBX proteins contribute to nucleolar relocalization.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic differences between truncated and full-length proteins

claim: There was a robust increase in GFP-CBX8 signal in nucleoli isolated from cells directly after HS.
source: Microscopic analysis of unfixed isolated nucleoli followed by image analysis showed a robust increase in GFP-CBX8 signal in nucleoli isolated for cells directly after HS (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and image analysis data shown in Figures 2B and 2C

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed an increase of GFP-CBX8 in the nucleolar fraction after HS.
source: Next, we performed western blot analysis on isolated cytoplasmic, nucleoplasmic and nucleoli fractions from GFP-CBX8 cells, which confirmed the presence of the nucleolar marker Fibrillarin in the nucleoli fraction and clearly showed an increase of GFP-CBX8 in the nucleolar fraction after HS (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Endogenous CBX4 was enriched in the nucleolar fraction after HS in K562 cells.
source: Clearly, both endogenous CBX4 and CBX8 were enriched in the nucleolar fraction after HS.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of cellular fractions

claim: Endogenous CBX8 was enriched in the nucleolar fraction after HS in K562 cells.
source: Clearly, both endogenous CBX4 and CBX8 were enriched in the nucleolar fraction after HS.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of cellular fractions

claim: Endogenous RING1B levels were slightly elevated in the nucleolar fraction after HS in K562 cells.
source: In addition, also endogenous RING1B levels were slightly elevated in the nucleolar fraction after HS.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of cellular fractions

claim: Endogenous CBX4, CBX8 and RING1B showed a robust shift to the nucleolus after HS in HL60 cells.
source: To validate these results in an independent cell line, we analyzed cellular fractions isolated from HL60 cells (Figure 2G). Also here, we observed a robust shift of endogenous CBX4, CBX8 and RING1B to the nucleolus after HS.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of cellular fractions shown in Figure 2G

claim: HS is known to lead to a general shutdown of transcription.
source: HS is known to lead to a general shutdown of transcription.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Cellular stressors like HS and proteasome inhibition induce a quick depletion of the free ubiquitin pool.
source: Cellular stressors like HS and proteasome inhibition induce a quick depletion of the free ubiquitin pool and this coincides with a quick reduction of ubiquitinated histone H2A (H2AK119ub) in the cell (Carlson and Rechsteiner, 1987; Dantuma et al., 2006; Mimnaugh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Depletion of the free ubiquitin pool coincides with a quick reduction of ubiquitinated histone H2A (H2AK119ub) in the cell.
source: Cellular stressors like HS and proteasome inhibition induce a quick depletion of the free ubiquitin pool and this coincides with a quick reduction of ubiquitinated histone H2A (H2AK119ub) in the cell (Carlson and Rechsteiner, 1987; Dantuma et al., 2006; Mimnaugh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: HS leads to dramatic alterations of the 3D chromatin architecture in Drosophila cells as a consequence of weakening insulators between topologically associating domains (TADs).
source: A study in Drosophila cells indeed showed that HS leads to dramatic alterations of the 3D chromatin architecture as a consequence of weakening insulators between topologically associating domains (TADs) and newly formed architectural protein binding sites (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Polycomb complexes were redistributed to active promoters/enhancers and formed inter-TAD interactions in Drosophila cells after HS, likely resulting in transcriptional silencing.
source: In addition, Polycomb complexes were redistributed to active promoters/enhancers and formed inter-TAD interactions, likely resulting in transcriptional silencing.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work with speculative interpretation

claim: For a subset of genes encoding heat-shock proteins (HSPs), HS does not cause a decrease but rather an increase in gene transcription.
source: For a subset of genes, however, in particular the genes encoding the heat-shock proteins (HSPs), HS does not cause a decrease but rather an increase in gene transcription.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the heat shock response

claim: The Heat Shock Response is mediated largely by Heat Shock Transcription factor-1 (HSF-1).
source: This response is referred to as the Heat Shock Response and mediated largely by the so-called Heat Shock Transcription factor-1 (HSF-1) (Akerfelt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: HSPs function as molecular chaperones, guiding co-translational folding under normal conditions and serving to refold heat-unfolded proteins.
source: HSPs function as molecular chaperones, not only guiding co-translational folding under normal conditions but also serving to refold heat-unfolded proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HSP function

claim: If proteins cannot be correctly refolded, they can be poly-ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome.
source: If proteins cannot be correctly refolded, they can be poly-ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of protein quality control

claim: The intracellular pool of 'free' ubiquitin that is used for poly-ubiquitination of proteins is limited.
source: Importantly, the intracellular pool of 'free' ubiquitin that is used for poly-ubiquitination of proteins is limited (Carlson and Rechsteiner, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: HSPs prevent protein dysfunction and aggregation, a hallmark of various age-related neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.
source: As such, HSPs prevent protein dysfunction and aggregation, a hallmark of various age-related neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (Hartl et al., 2011; Kampinga and Bergink, 2016; Morimoto, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis identified 1279 proteins in the nucleolar proteome.
source: In total, we identified 1279 proteins, and the nucleolar proteins NPM1 and Fibrillarin were among the most abundant proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in supplementary figure

claim: NPM1 and Fibrillarin were among the most abundant proteins in the nucleolar proteome.
source: In total, we identified 1279 proteins, and the nucleolar proteins NPM1 and Fibrillarin were among the most abundant proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in supplementary figure

claim: GO term analysis of the top ten percent identified proteins showed strong enrichment for GO terms related to ribosome biogenesis and rRNA processing.
source: GO term analysis of the top ten percent identified proteins based of LFQ values showed strong enrichment for GO terms related to ribosome biogenesis and rRNA processing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis data shown in supplementary figure

claim: MaxQuant-based label-free quantification resulted in the identification of 153 significantly enriched proteins in the nucleolus after HS.
source: MaxQuant-based label-free quantification of two independent experiments measured in triplicate resulted in the identification of 153 significantly enriched proteins in the nucleolus after HS and six depleted proteins (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary files 1–2).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data shown in figures and supplementary files

claim: Six proteins were depleted from the nucleolus after HS.
source: MaxQuant-based label-free quantification of two independent experiments measured in triplicate resulted in the identification of 153 significantly enriched proteins in the nucleolus after HS and six depleted proteins (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary files 1–2).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data shown in figures and supplementary files

claim: Nucleolar proteins like Fibrillarin and NPM1 were not affected by HS.
source: Nucleolar proteins like Fibrillarin and NPM1 were not affected by HS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Proteins enriched in the nucleolus after HS associated with GO terms related to chromatin modification, gene expression, DNA repair, histone ubiquitination and protein refolding.
source: Interestingly, proteins enriched in the nucleolus after HS associated with GO terms related to chromatin modification, gene expression, DNA repair, histone ubiquitination and protein refolding (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis of LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Various PRC1 subunits, including CBX2, RING1A, RING1B and PHC2 were significantly enriched in the nucleolus upon HS.
source: Consistent with our IF and biochemical fractionation data, various PRC1 subunits, including CBX2, RING1A, RING1B and PHC2 were significantly enriched in the nucleolus upon HS (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figure

claim: PRC2 subunits EZH2, SUZ12 and EED were enriched in the nucleolus upon HS.
source: Intriguingly, we also found that PRC2 subunits EZH2, SUZ12 and EED were enriched (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figure

claim: HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of EZH2 and SUZ12 was confirmed using western blot analysis on nucleolar fractions isolated from K562 or HL60 cells.
source: and this HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of EZH2 and SUZ12 was confirmed using western blot analysis on nucleolar fractions isolated from K562 or HL60 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D

claim: HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of EZH2 was independently confirmed using immunofluorescence analyses in K562 cells, HL60 cells, and primary non-transformed CD34+ mobilized peripheral blood stem cells (mPBSCs).
source: HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of EZH2 was independently confirmed using immunofluorescence analyses in K562 cells, HL60 cells, and primary non-transformed CD34+mobilized peripheral blood stem cells (mPBSCs) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in supplementary figures

claim: Intra-nucleolar levels of H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub were not increased in heat shocked cells versus untreated cells.
source: Intra-nucleolar levels of H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub were not increased in heat shocked cells versus untreated cells, suggesting that PcG proteins are not involved in Polycomb-mediated silencing of nucleolar chromatin (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E

claim: PcG proteins are not involved in Polycomb-mediated silencing of nucleolar chromatin after HS.
source: Intra-nucleolar levels of H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub were not increased in heat shocked cells versus untreated cells, suggesting that PcG proteins are not involved in Polycomb-mediated silencing of nucleolar chromatin (Figure 3E).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increase in H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub in nucleoli

claim: Members of the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding (CHD) family were found to be enriched in the nucleolus after HS.
source: In addition to these PcG proteins, many other chromatin and transcription regulating proteins were found to be enriched in the nucleolus after HS, including members of the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding (CHD) family and the FACT chromatin remodeling complex that both can remodel chromatin (Marfella and Imbalzano, 2007; Winkler and Luger, 2011), and the PAF complex, which regulates release of RNAPII into processive elongation (Van Oss et al., 2017) (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figure, with citations to published work on CHD function

claim: The FACT chromatin remodeling complex was enriched in the nucleolus after HS.
source: In addition to these PcG proteins, many other chromatin and transcription regulating proteins were found to be enriched in the nucleolus after HS, including members of the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding (CHD) family and the FACT chromatin remodeling complex that both can remodel chromatin (Marfella and Imbalzano, 2007; Winkler and Luger, 2011), and the PAF complex, which regulates release of RNAPII into processive elongation (Van Oss et al., 2017) (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figure, with citations to published work on FACT function

claim: The PAF complex was enriched in the nucleolus after HS.
source: In addition to these PcG proteins, many other chromatin and transcription regulating proteins were found to be enriched in the nucleolus after HS, including members of the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding (CHD) family and the FACT chromatin remodeling complex that both can remodel chromatin (Marfella and Imbalzano, 2007; Winkler and Luger, 2011), and the PAF complex, which regulates release of RNAPII into processive elongation (Van Oss et al., 2017) (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figure, with citation to published work on PAF function

claim: Accumulation of BRD proteins and JMJD6 was observed in the nucleolus after HS.
source: In addition, accumulation of BRD proteins and JMJD6 was observed in the nucleolus after HS (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3G and supplementary figure

claim: BRD4 and JMJD6 are co-bound to enhancers and regulate promoter-proximal pause-release of RNAPII.
source: BRD4 and JMJD6 are co-bound to enhancers and regulate promoter-proximal pause-release of RNAPII (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: HS induces strong shifts of various chromatin and transcription regulators toward the nucleolus.
source: Taken together, these data show that HS induces strong shifts of various chromatin and transcription regulators toward the nucleolus.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive LC-MS/MS data

claim: Several chaperone proteins were enriched in the nucleolus after HS, including members of the HSP70 chaperone family (HSPA1A/B), DNAJB1, DNAJC7 and the small heat shock protein HSPB1.
source: In line with our western analysis of cellular fractions, our proteomic analyses showed several chaperone proteins to be enriched in the nucleolus after HS. These included members of the HSP70 chaperone family (HSPA1A/B), DNAJB1, DNAJC7 and the small heat shock protein HSPB1 (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3H and supplementary figure

claim: Many other chaperones, including members of the HSP90 family were not or weakly enriched in the nucleolus after HS.
source: Strikingly, many other chaperones, including members of the HSP90 family were not or weakly enriched in the nucleolus after HS showing the response is specific and suggesting that this subset of HSPs may somehow have functional implications in this response.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data

claim: A strong accumulation of 26S proteasome subunits was observed in the nucleolus after HS.
source: In addition to the HSPs, we also observed a strong accumulation of 26S proteasome subunits in the nucleolus after HS (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3I and supplementary figure

claim: Post-HS proteasomal degradation of damaged proteins may occur in the nucleolus.
source: It is possible that post-HS proteasomal degradation of damaged proteins occurs in the nucleolus.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of proteasome accumulation data

claim: Model proteins are targeted to the nucleolus for post-stress degradation.
source: This is consistent with observations using model proteins, which are targeted to the nucleolus for post-stress degradation (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Independent LC-MS/MS analysis with K562 GFP-CBX8 cells confirmed HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of various chromatin regulators, protein chaperones and proteasomal subunits.
source: Independent LC-MS/MS analysis with K562 GFP-CBX8 cells confirmed these findings, implying that HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of various chromatin regulators, protein chaperones and proteasomal subunits is a conserved biological phenomenon (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by independent LC-MS/MS data shown in supplementary figures

claim: HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of various chromatin regulators, protein chaperones and proteasomal subunits is a conserved biological phenomenon.
source: Independent LC-MS/MS analysis with K562 GFP-CBX8 cells confirmed these findings, implying that HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of various chromatin regulators, protein chaperones and proteasomal subunits is a conserved biological phenomenon (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Inferred from reproducibility across independent experiments

claim: Upon HS many chromatin remodelers and transcriptional regulators accumulate in the nucleolus which may become a hot spot for protein quality control.
source: Our data suggests that upon HS many chromatin remodelers and transcriptional regulators accumulate in the nucleolus which may become a hot spot for protein quality control.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the comprehensive data

claim: Upon HS (1 hr, 44°C) a strong reduction in chromatin binding of GFP-CBX2, BMI1-GFP, MEL18-GFP and, to a lesser extent, GFP-RING1B was observed.
source: Indeed, upon HS (1 hr, 44°C) we observed a strong reduction in chromatin binding of GFP-CBX2, BMI1-GFP, MEL18-GFP and, to a lesser extent, GFP-RING1B (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A

claim: A quick reduction in CBX8 binding to Polycomb target genes was observed after HS.
source: To investigate how HS impacts on chromatin binding of endogenous PRC1 subunits, we performed ChIPs using an antibody directed against endogenous CBX8, and also here we observed a quick reduction in CBX8 binding to Polycomb target genes after HS (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B

claim: ChIP analysis using an antibody directed against the PRC2 subunit EZH2 showed a loss of endogenous EZH2 binding from target genes after HS.
source: Moreover, in line with our LC-MS/MS data, ChIP analysis using an antibody directed against the PRC2 subunit EZH2 also clearly showed a loss of endogenous EZH2 binding from target genes after HS, confirming that both PRC1 and PRC2 show strongly reduced chromatin binding after HS (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Both PRC1 and PRC2 show strongly reduced chromatin binding after HS.
source: Moreover, in line with our LC-MS/MS data, ChIP analysis using an antibody directed against the PRC2 subunit EZH2 also clearly showed a loss of endogenous EZH2 binding from target genes after HS, confirming that both PRC1 and PRC2 show strongly reduced chromatin binding after HS (Figure 4C).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP data for both PRC1 and PRC2 subunits

claim: Previous studies have shown that HS induces a rapid but reversible loss of ubiquitinated histones.
source: Previous studies have shown that HS induces a rapid but reversible loss of ubiquitinated histones (Carlson et al., 1987; Mimnaugh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: A strong decrease in H2AK119ub levels was observed after HS.
source: Indeed, we also observed a strong decrease in H2AK119ub levels after HS (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D

claim: H3K27me3 levels were significantly reduced in heat-shocked cells vs. control cells.
source: In addition, H3K27me3 levels were also significantly reduced in heat-shocked cells vs. control cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E

claim: HS causes displacement of PRC1/2 complexes and leads to a reduction of their respective epimarks.
source: These data show that HS not only causes displacement of PRC1/2 complexes but also leads to a reduction of their respective epimarks.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP data showing both loss of binding and loss of marks

claim: Heat maps and band plots of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 peaks showed a loss of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 chromatin binding after HS.
source: Heat maps and band plots of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 peaks clearly showed a loss of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 chromatin binding after HS (Figure 4F and G, Supplementary files 4–5).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 4F and 4G

claim: Many CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 peaks were found to be intergenic.
source: In line with our previous observations concerning PRC1 chromatin occupancy, many CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 peaks were found to be intergenic (van den Boom et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in supplementary figure, with citation to published work

claim: A loss of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 chromatin association at gene promoters is observed upon HS.
source: To investigate HS-induced reduction of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 at gene promoters, we generated heat maps and band plots of transcription start site (TSS)-associated peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C). Clearly, also here a loss of CBX8 and GFP-CBX2 chromatin association is observed upon HS.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: TSS-localized peaks are associated to genes enriched for development-related GO terms, confirming that these are Polycomb target genes.
source: TSS-localized peaks are associated to genes enriched for development-related GO terms, confirming that these are Polycomb target genes (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4H

claim: After HS (1 hr, 44°C) H3K4me3 levels are reduced.
source: Here we find that, in addition to loss of H2AK119ub and H3K27me3, after HS (1 hr, 44°C) also H3K4me3 levels are reduced, and, likely as a consequence of H3K4me3 loss, H3K4me1 levels are increased (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4J

claim: H3K4me1 levels are increased after HS, likely as a consequence of H3K4me3 loss.
source: Here we find that, in addition to loss of H2AK119ub and H3K27me3, after HS (1 hr, 44°C) also H3K4me3 levels are reduced, and, likely as a consequence of H3K4me3 loss, H3K4me1 levels are increased (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4J, with speculative interpretation

claim: The increase in H3K4me1 levels argues that loss of epimarks is not a mere consequence of decreased nucleosome occupancy but truly a consequence of changes in the epigenetic marking of the chromatin.
source: The increase in H3K4me1 levels argues that loss of epimarks is not a mere consequence of decreased nucleosome occupancy but truly a consequence of changes in the epigenetic marking of the chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K4me1 increases while other marks decrease

claim: The expression of various Polycomb target genes was increased 3 hr after HS, and recovered to pre-HS levels afterwards.
source: Finally, we investigated whether the HS-induced loss of PRC1/2-associated epimarks also resulted in loss of silencing of Polycomb target genes. Indeed, we found that the expression of various Polycomb target genes was increased 3 hr after HS, and recovered to pre-HS levels afterwards (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by qPCR expression data shown in Figure 4K

claim: In parallel to the reallocation of chromatin remodelers and transcriptional regulators to the nucleolus, HS induces a quick reduction in PRC1 and PRC2 chromatin binding and changes in the epigenetic profile of PcG target genes with consequences for the transcriptional state of these genes.
source: Taken together, these data show that, in parallel to the reallocation of chromatin remodelers and transcriptional regulators to the nucleolus, HS induces a quick reduction in PRC1 and PRC2 chromatin binding and changes in the epigenetic profile of PcG target genes with consequences for the transcriptional state of these genes.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive ChIP and expression data

claim: The kinetics of nucleolar GFP-CBX2 in untreated cells were very quick.
source: Strikingly, whereas the kinetics of nucleolar GFP-CBX2 in untreated cells were very quick, nucleolar GFP-CBX2 was highly immobile in heat shocked cells (Figure 5B and C) with limited to no dynamic exchange between the nucleolus and the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figures 5B and 5C

claim: Nucleolar GFP-CBX2 was highly immobile in heat shocked cells with limited to no dynamic exchange between the nucleolus and the nucleoplasm.
source: Strikingly, whereas the kinetics of nucleolar GFP-CBX2 in untreated cells were very quick, nucleolar GFP-CBX2 was highly immobile in heat shocked cells (Figure 5B and C) with limited to no dynamic exchange between the nucleolus and the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figures 5B and 5C

claim: The nucleolus is a membrane-less nuclear body with liquid-like properties; its formation depends on liquid-liquid phase transition.
source: The nucleolus is a membrane-less nuclear body with liquid-like properties; its formation depends on liquid-liquid phase transition (Brangwynne et al., 2011; Marko, 2012).

claim: There was very little fluorescence recovery in the bleached region and fluorescence loss in the adjacent nucleolar region in heat shocked cells, indicating that GFP-CBX2 might be present in these nucleoli in a more solid-like state.

claim: Proteins in similar solid states have been shown to be aggregated.

evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Both GFP-CBX2 and GFP-CBX8 nucleolar accumulations were 1,6-hexanediol insensitive.
source: Clearly, both GFP-CBX2 and GFP-CBX8 nucleolar accumulations were 1,6-hexanediol insensitive (Figure 5F and G), in line with a more solid, aggregation-like state.
evidence: Supported by 1,6-hexanediol treatment data shown in Figures 5F and 5G

claim: 1,6-hexanediol insensitivity is in line with a more solid, aggregation-like state.
source: Clearly, both GFP-CBX2 and GFP-CBX8 nucleolar accumulations were 1,6-hexanediol insensitive (Figure 5F and G), in line with a more solid, aggregation-like state.
evidence: Inferred from the 1,6-hexanediol insensitivity data

claim: Within 3 hr after HS the GFP-CBX2 nucleolar accumulations dispersed and GFP-CBX2 regained its original pan-nuclear distribution.
source: Clearly, within 3 hr after HS the GFP-CBX2 nucleolar accumulations dispersed and GFP-CBX2 regained its original pan-nuclear distribution (Figure 6A), showing that nucleolar accumulations of PcG proteins are readily reversible.
evidence: Supported by time-course microscopy data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Nucleolar accumulations of PcG proteins are readily reversible.
source: Clearly, within 3 hr after HS the GFP-CBX2 nucleolar accumulations dispersed and GFP-CBX2 regained its original pan-nuclear distribution (Figure 6A), showing that nucleolar accumulations of PcG proteins are readily reversible.
evidence: Inferred from the recovery data

claim: DNAJB1 showed reversible HS-induced nucleolar accumulation.
source: Similarly, and in line with our cellular fraction data and LC-MS/MS data, we also observed a reversible HS-induced nucleolar accumulation of DNAJB1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: HSP70 showed post-HS nuclear translocation, and localized to the nucleolus in a reversible fashion.

evidence: Inferred from comparison of immunofluorescence and LC-MS/MS data

claim: Post-HS nucleolar accumulation was not impaired upon HSP70 inhibition, suggesting that the HSP70 machinery is not involved in chaperoning PcG proteins to the nucleolus after HS.
source: Clearly, post-HS nucleolar accumulation was not impaired upon HSP70 inhibition, suggesting that the HSP70 machinery is not involved in chaperoning PcG proteins to the nucleolus after HS (Figure 6B).

claim: HSP70 inhibition led to a clear delay in recovery of GFP-CBX2 from the nucleoli suggesting that HSP70 activity is required to resolve the nucleolar accumulation of GFP-CBX2.
source: However, HSP70 inhibition led to a clear delay in recovery of GFP-CBX2 from the nucleoli suggesting that HSP70 activity is required to resolve the nucleolar accumulation of GFP-CBX2 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by HSP70 inhibitor treatment data shown in Figures 6B and 6C

claim: A partial knockdown of HSPA1A resulted in a significant delay of GFP-CBX2 recovery from the nucleoli in HEK293T GFP-CBX2 cells.

claim: HS is known to induce HSP expression (including several HSP70s), resulting in a period of increased thermotolerance.
source: HS is known to induce HSP expression (including several HSP70s), resulting in a period of increased thermotolerance.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the heat shock response

claim: Recovery of GFP-CBX2 after the first HS required almost 3 hr, whereas recovery after the second HS was almost completed within 30 min.
source: Indeed, whereas recovery of GFP-CBX2 after the first HS required almost 3 hr, recovery after the second HS was almost completed within 30 min (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by thermotolerance experiment data shown in Figures 6E and 6F

claim: The amount of GFP-CBX2 that initially accumulated during the first or second HS did not change dramatically.
source: Importantly, the amount of GFP-CBX2 that initially accumulated during the first or second HS did not change dramatically (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by thermotolerance experiment data shown in Figures 6E and 6F

claim: Increased HSP levels specifically affect the recovery of GFP-CBX2 proteins from the solid phase within the nucleolus.
source: This implies that increased HSP levels specifically affect the recovery of GFP-CBX2 proteins from the solid phase within the nucleolus.
evidence: Inferred from the thermotolerance experiment showing faster recovery with elevated HSP levels

claim: H2AK119ub was completely recovered at 4 hr after HS.

claim: H3K27me3 recovery was slightly delayed compared to H2AK119ub.
source: Indeed, we found that H2AK119ub was completely recovered at 4 hr after HS, whereas H3K27me3 recovery was slightly delayed (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G

claim: At later time points after HS there was a complete recovery of GFP-CBX2 and various epigenetic modifications.
source: At later time points after HS we observed a complete recovery of GFP-CBX2 and various epigenetic modifications (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in supplementary figure

claim: H2AK119ub recovery was strongly dependent on HSP protein expression.
source: Interestingly, H2AK119ub recovery was strongly dependent on HSP protein expression.
evidence: Inferred from thermotolerance experiment data

claim: HSP70 and DNAJB1 were strongly induced upon the first HS.

evidence: Supported by western blot data

claim: EZH2 and CBX8 protein levels were rather stable or slightly reduced after HS.
source: In line with our ChIP-qPCR data, H3K27me3 was also reduced albeit with slower kinetics. Both HSP70 and DNAJB1 were strongly induced upon the first HS, whereas EZH2 and CBX8 protein levels were rather stable or slightly reduced.
evidence: Supported by western blot data

claim: Post-HS H2AK119ub recovery is dependent on Polycomb proteins that are recovered from the nucleolus and not merely on newly translated Polycomb proteins.
source: Next, we investigated whether post-HS H2AK119ub recovery is dependent on Polycomb proteins that are recovered from the nucleolus and not merely on newly translated Polycomb proteins.
evidence: This is the research question being tested

claim: H2AK119ub recovery did not depend on de novo protein synthesis as H2AK119ub levels also recovered in cycloheximide-treated cells.
source: Importantly, H2AK119ub recovery did not depend on de novo protein synthesis as H2AK119ub levels also recovered in cycloheximide-treated cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide treatment data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Molecular chaperones are crucial for recovery of GFP-CBX2 from the nucleolus.
source: Taken together, these data show that molecular chaperones are crucial for recovery of GFP-CBX2 from the nucleolus and that this activity is essential for epigenetic recovery after HS (Figure 6I).

claim: Molecular chaperone activity is essential for epigenetic recovery after HS.
source: Taken together, these data show that molecular chaperones are crucial for recovery of GFP-CBX2 from the nucleolus and that this activity is essential for epigenetic recovery after HS (Figure 6I).
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive recovery experiments

claim: Spatial separation of proteins in the cytosol and nucleus upon heat stress has been repeatedly suggested to prevent interference of un- or misfolded proteins with essential cellular processes.
source: Spatial separation of proteins in the cytosol and nucleus upon heat stress has been repeatedly suggested to prevent interference of un- or misfolded proteins with essential cellular processes (Escusa-Toret et al., 2013; Kaganovich et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Spatial separation may allow for rapid recovery of proteins to re-initiate the crucial processes they are normally engaged in.
source: At the same time, this 'storage' may allow for rapid recovery of proteins to re-initiate the crucial processes they are normally engaged in.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the concept of spatial separation

claim: Studies with reporter proteins revealed that HS-induced redistribution to the nucleolus is important for both refolding or degradation of these reporters.
source: For the nucleolus, these experiments have been done with reporter proteins, without any direct connection to physiological cellular processes. Despite this drawback, these studies revealed that HS-induced redistribution to the nucleolus is important for both refolding (Nollen et al., 2001) or degradation (Park et al., 2013) of these reporters.
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: This study is the first to show that numerous endogenous chromatin regulators temporarily accumulate in the nucleolus upon a HS, and, in an HSP70-dependent manner, fully and functionally recover to the chromatin upon return to physiological temperatures.
source: Our data are the first to show that numerous endogenous chromatin regulators temporarily accumulate in the nucleolus upon a HS, and, in an HSP70-dependent manner, fully and functionally recover to the chromatin upon return to physiological temperatures.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive data presented in the study

claim: A ncRNA, arising from intergenic stretches in between ribosomal DNA repeats, is capable of sequestering and immobilizing various proteins in the nucleolus upon acidosis or HS.
source: Data from Audas and colleagues showed that a ncRNA, arising from intergenic stretches in between ribosomal DNA repeats, is capable of sequestering and immobilizing various proteins in the nucleolus upon acidosis or HS (Audas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Heat-unfolded nuclear reporter proteins have been reported to accumulate in the nucleolus via chaperoned transport.
source: Alternatively or in parallel, heat-unfolded nuclear reporter proteins (Nollen et al., 2001) or cytosolic proteins (Park et al., 2013) have been reported to accumulate in the nucleolus via chaperoned transport.
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The appearance of PcG proteins in the nucleolus were independent of the HSP70 machinery.
source: Whilst we cannot exclude this possibility here, the appearance of PcG proteins in the nucleolus were independent of the HSP70 machinery.
evidence: Supported by HSP70 inhibition data

claim: Both HSPA1A/HSP70 knockdown and inhibiting HSP70 activity result in a significant delay of GFP-CBX2 recovery from the nucleolus.
source: We also show that both HSPA1A/HSP70 knockdown and inhibiting HSP70 activity result in a significant delay of GFP-CBX2 recovery from the nucleolus, whereas elevated HSP70 expression accelerates the reallocation of PcG proteins to the chromatin.
evidence: Supported by knockdown and inhibitor data

claim: Elevated HSP70 expression accelerates the reallocation of PcG proteins to the chromatin.
source: We also show that both HSPA1A/HSP70 knockdown and inhibiting HSP70 activity result in a significant delay of GFP-CBX2 recovery from the nucleolus, whereas elevated HSP70 expression accelerates the reallocation of PcG proteins to the chromatin.
evidence: Supported by thermotolerance experiment data

claim: Post-HS GFP-CBX2 accumulations are 1,6-hexanediol insensitive, suggesting that it is present in the nucleolus in a more solid phase.
source: Whereas the nucleolus is a membrane-less organelle with liquid-like properties (Brangwynne et al., 2011; Marko, 2012), our finding that post-HS GFP-CBX2 accumulations are 1,6-hexanediol insensitive, suggest that it is present in the nucleolus in a more solid phase.
evidence: Inferred from 1,6-hexanediol treatment data with reference to published work on nucleolar properties

claim: The requirement of an active HSP70 machinery for re-solubilization could relate to GFP-CBX2 being present in a solid phase.
source: This could relate to the requirement of an active HSP70 machinery for its re-solubilization upon recovery.
evidence: Speculative interpretation linking solid phase to HSP70 requirement

claim: Both HSP70 and DNAJB1 that accumulate in the nucleolus are crucial components of chaperone machines with protein disaggregation power capable of functionally solubilizing proteins.
source: In fact, both HSP70 and DNAJB1 that accumulate in the nucleolus are crucial components of chaperone machines with protein disaggregation power capable of functionally solubilizing proteins (Mogk et al., 2018; Nillegoda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The functional recovery of epigenetic control was not dependent on de novo synthesis of the PcG proteins.

evidence: Supported by cycloheximide treatment data

claim: At least a large fraction of nucleolar PcG proteins are re-solubilized and functionally refolded.
source: Translation inhibition did not interfere with this H2AK119ub recovery, suggesting that a least a large fraction of nucleolar PcG proteins are re-solubilized and functionally refolded.
evidence: Inferred from cycloheximide treatment data showing recovery without new protein synthesis

claim: A fraction of the nucleolar accumulated proteins may be targeted for proteasomal degradation supported by the HS-induced nucleolar enrichment of the 26S proteasome.
source: In addition, a fraction of the nucleolar accumulated proteins may be targeted for proteasomal degradation supported by the HS-induced nucleolar enrichment of the 26S proteasome that we found.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of proteasome accumulation data

evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Other types of stress such as transcription inhibition, DNA damage induction and viral infection have been shown to cause major changes in the protein composition of the nucleolus.

claim: HS mainly induced accumulation of proteins in the nucleolus, whereas transcription inhibition using actinomycin D resulted in a release of ribosomal proteins and RNA processing factors and an increase of snRNP proteins.

evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Treatment of cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 led to an increase in ribosomal proteins in the nucleolus.
source: In contrast, treatment of cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132, which similarly to HS leads to proteotoxic stress, led to an increase in ribosomal proteins in the nucleolus (Andersen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The nucleolus could be an important protein quality control center serving under many different stress conditions.
source: Together, these data suggest that the nucleolus could be an important protein quality control center serving under many different stress conditions.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of different stress responses

claim: Proteotoxic stress-induced loss of H2AK119ub has previously been observed by other groups.
source: Proteotoxic stress-induced loss of H2AK119ub has previously been observed by other groups (Carlson and Rechsteiner, 1987; Dantuma et al., 2006; Mimnaugh et al., 1997), and it has been proposed that the reason for this loss is the urgent need for 'free' ubiquitin in cells post-HS.
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: It has been proposed that the reason for H2AK119ub loss is the urgent need for 'free' ubiquitin in cells post-HS.
source: Proteotoxic stress-induced loss of H2AK119ub has previously been observed by other groups (Carlson and Rechsteiner, 1987; Dantuma et al., 2006; Mimnaugh et al., 1997), and it has been proposed that the reason for this loss is the urgent need for 'free' ubiquitin in cells post-HS.
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: HS-induced redistribution of PcG proteins to the nucleolus has direct implications for histone marking and is not limited to H2AK119ub, but also affects H3K27me3, H3K4me3 and H3K4me1 levels at PcG target genes.
source: Our data suggests that HS-induced redistribution of PcG proteins to the nucleolus has direct implications for histone marking and is not limited to H2AK119ub, but also affects H3K27me3, H3K4me3 and H3K4me1 levels at PcG target genes.

claim: Other studies have shown HS-induced loss of H3K27Ac from HS-repressed enhancers.

claim: A moderate localization of the Drosophila Polycomb (Pc) protein to the nucleolus upon HS was observed.

evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Although ribosomal DNA transcription in the nucleolus was strongly reduced upon HS, Pc binding to ribosomal DNA repeats was not increased, suggesting that Pc is not involved in repressing ribosomal DNA transcription.

evidence: Supported by citation to published work

source: Together these findings contradict a hypothetical chromatin regulatory activity of PRC1/2 in the nucleolus after HS but rather suggest that their respective subunits are undergoing protein quality control.

claim: HS directly affects chromatin binding of PcG proteins and results in a decrease of PcG-related epigenetic modifications.
source: Taken together, our data shows that HS directly affects chromatin binding of PcG proteins and results in a decrease of PcG-related epigenetic modifications.

claim: HSP70-dependent protein disaggregation and refolding enables PcG proteins to quickly re-initiate their epigenetic functions at target genes.
source: Importantly, HSP70-dependent protein disaggregation and refolding enables PcG proteins to quickly re-initiate their epigenetic functions at target genes.

claim: Despite the fact that the majority of epimarks may be properly reinstalled, mistakes will result in epigenetic scars, which may contribute to cellular transformation, loss of cell function and ultimately cell death.

Despite the fact that the majority of epimarks may be properly reinstalled, mistakes will result in epigenetic scars, which may contribute to cellular transformation, loss of cell function and ultimately cell death.

claim: Various studies have shown that alterations in transcriptional and epigenetic regulation are major contributors to aging-associated loss of cellular function.
source: Various studies have shown that alterations in transcriptional and epigenetic regulation are major contributors to aging-associated loss of cellular function (Booth and Brunet, 2016).

claim: Cellular-stress-induced epigenetic changes may contribute to age-associated epigenetic alterations.
